notes.meaning: Gideon and his army camped early in the morning by the spring of Harod, while the Midianites were camped below them in the valley near the hill of Moreh. Gideon moved quickly because God had already encouraged him with signs. Holding the higher ground by the spring gave Israel a safe position looking down on the enemy.

The Lord told Gideon that his army of thirty-two thousand men was far too large. If such a big force won the battle, the Israelites would boast that their own strength had saved them. God wanted His people to see clearly that victory comes only from Him.

God directed Gideon to tell anyone who felt afraid to leave and head home. Twenty-two thousand men walked away, leaving just ten thousand behind. Fear can spread quickly through an army, and God's law already excused frightened soldiers from going to war.

The Lord told Gideon that ten thousand men were still too many. He instructed Gideon to lead them to the water, where God would test them and choose who would fight. The final selection would depend entirely on God's choice rather than human military planning.

Gideon brought the men to the water, and the Lord told him to divide them into two groups. One group would be those who lapped water with their tongues like a dog, and the other would be those who got down on their knees to drink. God used this simple daily habit to separate the soldiers He wanted.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars propose that lapping water like a dog was a symbolic image of fierce warriors eager to lap up the blood of their enemies in battle.

notes.meaning: Only three hundred men brought water up to their mouths with their hands, while all the other ninety-seven hundred knelt flat to drink. The three hundred stayed on their feet and kept watch while taking a quick drink. The vast majority put their faces right to the water without watching their surroundings.

The Lord promised Gideon that He would rescue Israel and defeat Midian using only the three hundred men who lapped. Everyone else was ordered to pack up and go home. Gideon trusted God's promise even though his army had become tiny.

Gideon sent the rest of Israel home but kept the three hundred men, collecting the extra food jars and ram horns left behind. Meanwhile, the huge Midianite camp rested below in the valley. Having these supplies ensured that every single one of Gideon's three hundred fighters had a trumpet.

That night the Lord ordered Gideon to go down and attack the Midianite camp because He had already handed it over to him. God spoke of the victory as something already guaranteed. Even before the fight started, the outcome was settled in God's plan.

The Lord told Gideon that if he still felt afraid to attack, he should first sneak down to the enemy camp with his servant Purah. God kindly offered comfort instead of scolding Gideon for his hesitation. God patiently builds up the faith of His servants when they feel weak.

God promised that hearing what the Midianites were saying would give Gideon courage to lead the attack. Gideon and Purah slipped quietly down to the edge of the enemy camp where armed guards stood watch. The sprawling camp made it easy for them to get close without being spotted.

The Midianites, Amalekites, and other eastern nomadic tribes filled the valley like a thick swarm of locusts. Their camels were as countless as grains of sand on the beach. This massive number highlighted how impossible an Israelite victory would be without God's help.

Just as Gideon arrived, he heard a soldier telling a friend about a dream where a round loaf of barley bread rolled into camp and slammed into a tent until it collapsed. Barley bread was the food of poor farmers and seemed weak and harmless. Yet in the dream, this humble loaf completely smashed the tent of a desert warrior.

The soldier's comrade answered that the dream could only mean the sword of Gideon, because God had handed Midian and the entire camp over to him. Even the enemy soldiers had come to fear Gideon and Israel's God. God used the words of a foreign guard to confirm His promise of victory.

When Gideon heard the dream and its meaning, he bowed his head and worshipped the Lord right there. Then he hurried back to Israel's camp and told his men to get up because God had given them the victory. Giving thanks to God filled Gideon with fresh confidence for the mission.

Gideon split his three hundred men into three separate groups and gave each soldier a horn and an empty clay jar with a burning torch inside. Dividing the force created the illusion that a massive army was surrounding the camp. The jars kept the fire hidden until the exact moment of attack.

Gideon told his men to watch him closely and copy whatever he did once he reached the edge of the camp. The entire plan depended on all three groups acting together at the exact same moment. Gideon showed courage by leading the attack from the front.

Gideon instructed them that when his group blew their horns, every man around the camp must blow his horn and shout, 'For the Lord and for Gideon!' Hearing horns on every side would convince the enemy that many thousands of troops had encircled them. Using Gideon's name added extra dread because the Midianites already feared him.

Gideon and his hundred men reached the edge of the camp around ten at night, just after the guards were changed. Suddenly they blasted their horns and smashed the clay jars in their hands. Striking in the middle of the night caught the camp off guard during a sleepy, confused moment.

All three companies blew their horns and smashed their jars, holding blazing torches in their left hands and horns in their right while shouting the battle cry. The sudden noise of breaking pottery, trumpet blasts, and flashing light broke the darkness all at once. The Midianites woke up terrified, thinking an enormous army had penetrated their camp.

Each Israelite held his position around the perimeter while the whole Midianite army panicked, shouted, and ran away. The Israelites did not even need to swing their swords because God threw the enemy into wild confusion. God fought the real battle while His people stood their ground.

As the three hundred horns kept sounding, the Lord caused the Midianites to turn their swords against one another throughout the camp. The terrified survivors ran away eastward toward the Jordan River. In the pitch blackness and panic, allied tribes could not tell friend from foe and destroyed themselves.

Israelite men from the nearby tribes of Naphtali, Asher, and Manasseh were quickly summoned to chase down the fleeing Midianites. These were likely troops who had been sent home earlier but had stayed close by. Once the Lord started the victory, the wider community joined in to complete the defeat of the enemy.

Gideon sent runners into the hills of Ephraim, urging that tribe to cut off the escape route at the shallow crossings of the Jordan River down to Beth-barah. The men of Ephraim mobilized quickly and took control of the river passes. Blocking the water crossings trapped the retreating invaders on the west side of the river.

The men of Ephraim captured and killed Oreb and Zeeb, two Midianite generals whose names meant 'Raven' and 'Wolf.' They executed them at a rock and a winepress that were named after them, and brought their heads to Gideon across the Jordan. Capturing these top commanders broke Midian's leadership and brought an end to their cruel raids.
